input.reason: All three baseline items were unassisted and correct (accuracy 1.00, above the preregistered 0.70–1.00 band), but every observation is tagged exposure=previously_practiced and provenance=practice. Practice performance can justify a transfer test; it cannot confirm the transfer hypothesis, and the predicted error pattern (factor-pair overgeneralization) was never put at risk because no item required reinterpreting a novel structure. Engagement is the sharper signal: 142s, no replay, confusion and hesitation flags, and a fun rating of 1/5 alongside perfect accuracy — the child was correct and unmoved, which means the instrument told us nothing about how far the reasoning stretches. Quest eligibility is open on independent-correct evidence, so the right move is an unseen-transfer Quest that forces equal-groups reasoning into an unfamiliar shape with real cost attached.
preserve: Unassisted response format with no scaffolds offered before an answer is committed
All three target strands present: equal groups, missing factor, and word-problem interpretation
Short total runtime — the child's answers came fast and the instrument should not pad
change: Replace previously-practiced festival items with unseen material the child has no rehearsed procedure for
Add a real, losable resource so a wrong factor choice costs something visible instead of just being marked wrong
Deliberately bait factor-pair overgeneralization by offering arrangements where the wrong pairing looks tidier than the right one
Give the mathematics something to do on screen — quantities that rearrange and are seen to be the same or not the same
testNext: Does equal-groups reasoning survive when the groups are not pre-labeled and must be chosen?
Does the learner recover a missing factor when the total is fixed and the group size is the unknown, rather than the count?
Does factor-pair overgeneralization appear when 4×6 and 6×4 place things in physically different, non-interchangeable spaces?
Does interpreting a word problem still hold when one sentence contains a distractor number that belongs to no factor?
nextEvidenceRequired: At least 4 target-aligned unassisted observations on unseen items
At least one missing-factor item where the unknown is group size, not group count
At least one item that presents a plausible wrong factor pair, with the child's choice recorded
At least one word-problem item containing an irrelevant number, with the child's stated interpretation captured
Engagement capture: time to first commit, retries used, and end-of-session fun rating
input.nextTitle: The Cargo Elevator Has One Trip Left
input.nextAcademicTarget: math.multiplication.transfer — equal-groups construction, missing-factor recovery (unknown group size), and word-problem interpretation with distractor quantities, on unseen material
input.nextMechanic: Loading puzzle: the child builds crate stacks into a fixed-shape elevator bay, choosing how many rows and how many per row, then commits the trip.
input.nextTheme: A supply elevator on a mountain research station. Weather is closing in. What gets loaded correctly goes up; what doesn't stays on the ledge until spring.
input.nextOpeningPurpose: Open on the loading bay with the storm timer already visible and a radio voice stating the day's manifest — so the child knows within five seconds that there is a fixed amount of space, a fixed amount of cargo, and a limited number of trips.
input.nextCreatorPrompt: Build a five-stage cargo-loading instrument for a 9-year-old on a mountain station elevator. The bay is a grid whose dimensions the child sets by dragging a row handle and a column handle; crates auto-fill the shape they define. The manifest states a total (e.g., "28 ration crates, all must ride"), and the child must find a row/column arrangement that holds exactly that many — no gaps, no overflow. Stage 1: total given, both dimensions free (equal groups, constructed not read). Stage 2: the bay is locked to a fixed number of rows and the total is given — the child must find how many go in each row (missing factor with group size unknown). Stage 3: two bays of different shapes, one holding 4 rows of 6 and one holding 6 rows of 4; only one physically fits through the elevator door, so the child must see that same product does not mean same shape. Stage 4: a radioed manifest in sentences, including one number that names something other than a factor ("crate 19 is the fragile one") — the child must extract the real factors. Stage 5: a full manifest with three cargo types and limited bay space, requiring the child to arrange all three in sequence before the storm timer runs out. Storm timer runs across the whole session, not per stage. Overloading the bay makes crates tumble off the ledge and they are gone for the run. Show a running "left behind" count that the child cannot clear. End with the station log listing exactly what made it up and what did not, in the child's own numbers.
input.nextStakesDesign: Cargo is genuinely lost. Every crate the child fails to load — through an arrangement that overflows or a trip committed with empty slots — falls to the ledge and is subtracted from the station's supply for the run, shown as a count that only ever grows. The final station log is the child's own doing, printed plainly. What is at risk is the completeness of the delivery: a child who reasons well sends everything up and reads a clean log; a child who guesses at factor pairs reads a log with holes in it and knows exactly which crates they dropped. The storm timer means dithering also costs cargo, so hesitation is not free.
input.nextFailureMode: A run ends badly when the storm closes and the elevator makes its last trip with cargo still on the ledge. That is a real ending — the log shows the shortfall, the run is over, and reaching it requires starting the load again from stage one. Two specific paths lead there: committing arrangements whose product overshoots the manifest, so crates tumble and are unrecoverable, and stalling long enough on the shared timer that later stages have no time left. The child can restart the whole run, but cannot undo a lost crate within one.
input.nextEscalation: Stage 1 gives the total and lets both dimensions move — nearly any correct pairing works, so the child learns the controls while succeeding. Stage 2 removes one degree of freedom: rows are bolted, so the answer is a single unknown factor. Stage 3 introduces the trap — two arrangements with identical products, only one that fits the door — and the storm timer starts visibly draining. Stage 4 buries the factors in spoken language with a decoy number. Stage 5 stacks three manifests into one shared bay under the last minutes of the timer, where an early overload leaves no room to recover later. Time pressure and information ambiguity both climb; the arithmetic stays within third-grade range throughout.
input.nextMechanicSpec: The child drags a handle on the right edge of the bay to set rows and a handle on the bottom edge to set columns; as they drag, crates snap into the grid in real time and a counter above the bay reads the current capacity against the manifest total. Tapping the elevator button commits the trip. On commit: if capacity equals the manifest, the bay rises with a clean chime and the log ticks up. If capacity is under, the doors close on a partial load and the leftover crates slide onto the ledge and stay there, greyed out, with the "left behind" counter incrementing. If capacity is over, the extra crates visibly topple off the platform edge before the doors close. The storm timer is a bar of snow filling the top of the screen; when it fills, the elevator departs automatically with whatever is in the bay, decided or not.
input.nextMathematicalHook: 4 rows of 6 and 6 rows of 4 hold exactly the same number of crates — and one of them will not fit through the door. The product is stubbornly the same while the shape is not, and a child who has only ever memorized that 4×6 equals 6×4 gets to feel, physically, the part that equality does not cover.
